title: Find the transaction holding your lock
hook: How do you find who's blocking whom with `pg_locks` and `pg_stat_activity`?

scenes.caption: An uncommitted update can block another update to the same row.
scenes.narration: In a disposable database, open two sessions. Hold an update uncommitted in session A, then update the same existing row in B to reproduce blocking.

items: Create the test table and row first
Leave A open only for this experiment

scenes.caption: pg_blocking_pids resolves lock blockers without a fragile self-join.
scenes.narration: From a third session, find backends reporting lock waits and ask PostgreSQL for their blocker identifiers. Inspect the blocker chain; the waiting query is usually the victim.

elements.text:
SELECT pid, wait_event,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blockers
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';

scenes.caption: A blocker may be idle in transaction while still holding locks.
scenes.narration: Look up the blocker state and transaction start time, then inspect its locks. Row conflicts often appear as transaction identifier waits, not obvious tuple rows.

items: idle in transaction can still block
Do not join locks on relation alone

scenes.caption: Canceling a query does not reliably end an idle open transaction.
scenes.narration: End session A's transaction and confirm B resumes. Canceling a query is different from ending its transaction; fix application transaction scope to prevent repeated blocking.

elements.text:
-- Session A: discard this lab update
ROLLBACK;
-- Session B should now finish.
-- Recheck pg_blocking_pids afterward.

items: Use deliberate timeouts for lock waits

takeaway: Find blocker PIDs, inspect their transactions, and release the owning transaction rather than guessing from slow queries.
